'''Kathryn "Kitty" Hach-Darrow''' (October 20, 1922 – June 4, 2020) was an American businesswoman and philanthropist who co-founded the [[Hach Company|Hach Chemical Company]] in 1947 with her first husband Clifford C. Hach (pronounced hɑ:k). She was essential to the company's expansion, flying her own plane to small airfields across the country to sell water purification kits. She became president, [[chief operating officer]], and CEO of the Hach company.<ref name="Profile">{{cite web|title=Kitty Hach-Darrow|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/kathryn-c-kitty-hach-darrow|website=Science History Institute|date=29 June 2016 |accessdate=21 March 2018}}</ref><ref name="Loveland">{{cite web |title=Hach co-founder, Loveland philanthropist Kitty Hach-Darrow dies at 97 |url=https://www.reporterherald.com/2020/06/09/hach-co-founder-loveland-philanthropist-kitty-hach-darrow-dies-at-97/ |website=Loveland Reporter-Herald |accessdate=12 June 2020|date=June 9, 2020}}</ref>

Kathryn Hach-Darrow was also the first woman director of the [[American Water Works Association]], an international non-profit working for better water quality.  She has been noted for philanthropic work as well as her entrepreneurial success, and has received a number of awards and honors as a result of her contributions to both business and chemistry.<ref name=HallOfFame />

==Early life and education==

Kathryn Carter was born in [[Bucklin, Missouri]], where her father was an automobile dealer.<ref name="Profile"/> He was also a pilot, flying his own Eagle Rock biplane.<ref name=CHFOralHistory /> Kitty's first ride in an airplane occurred at the age of 5, the beginning of her lifelong love of flying.<ref name=CHFOralHistory /> Her mother was a schoolteacher.<ref name="Profile"/>

The [[Great Depression]] was financially disastrous for the Carter family. Her father did not go bankrupt, but lost his business and his plane.  The family bought a farm in [[Triplett, Missouri]] and lived there during Kathryn's teens. Kathryn did well in school and earned money for college by raising and selling turkeys.<ref name="Profile"/> She initially attended [[Columbia College (Missouri)|Columbia College]], Missouri (then named Christian Female College),<ref name=CHFHachs /> before transferring to [[Iowa State University]] to study [[home economics]].<ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Kathryn C. Hach-Darrow |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/hach-darrow-kathryn-c|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="CHFOralHistory">{{cite book|first1=Arnold |last1=Thackray |first2=Arthur |last2=Daemmrich |title=Kathryn C. Hach-Darrow, Transcript of Interviews Conducted by Arnold Thackray and Arthur Daemmrich at Loveland, Colorado, and Seattle, Washington on 20 July 2002, 2 October 2003, and 8 February 2004 |date=8 February 2004 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/hach-darrow_kc_0255_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Science History Institute|Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref>

At [[Iowa State University]], Kitty met [[Nellie May Naylor]], a chemist in the home economics department who interested her in chemistry.<ref name=Icons />

==Marriage and work==

{{external media | width = 220px | float = right | headerimage= [[File:2,2 bipyridine for iron lavender color.png|220px]] | video1 = [https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/kathryn-c-kitty-hach-darrow "The water on this planet is all that we have. It needs to be cared for."], Kathryn Hach-Darrow, [[Science History Institute]]}}

Kathryn and her first husband Clifford C. Hach met as students at [[Iowa State University]], and married in 1943. "I knew right away that this guy was going to build a chemical company," she says. "He didn't care how big Dow was or how big DuPont was, he was going to build his own company."<ref name=CEN2012>{{cite news|last=Wang|first=Linda|title=C&EN Talks With Kathryn Hach-Darrow|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/90/i43/CEN-Talks-Kathryn-Hach-Darrow.html|accessdate=25 February 2014|newspaper=Chemical & Engineering News|date=22 October 2012}}</ref>

Clifford did not receive his bachelor's degree until 1947, because he and other students were co-opted to work on war-time projects at the university.<ref name=CHFHachs>{{cite web|title=Clifford C. Hach and Kathryn Hach-Darrow|url=http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/chemistry-in-history/themes/public-and-environmental-health/public-health-and-safety/hach-and-hach-darrow.aspx|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation|accessdate=25 February 2014 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160712164648/http://www.chemheritage.org/discover/online-resources/chemistry-in-history/themes/public-and-environmental-health/public-health-and-safety/hach-and-hach-darrow.aspx|archivedate=July 12, 2016}}</ref><ref name=Icons>{{cite news|title=Industry Icons|url=http://editiondigital.net/display_article.php?id=779344|accessdate=25 February 2014|newspaper=Water and Wastes Digest — 50th Anniversary Special Edition {{!}} 1961-2011|year=2011}}</ref>  It was difficult to find jobs after graduation.  Eventually, Clifford was hired part-time by a filtration company in [[Ames, Iowa]] to analyze water.  Seeing how the water-treatment plant worked gave Clifford the idea for a process and a product: a simplified method of analysis that would enable workers to treat water with powdered formulas rather than heavy chemical solutions.<ref name="Profile"/>

He raised startup money by selling the rights to another invention. The Walter Kidde fire extinguisher company had approached the [[University of Iowa]] for ideas for generating carbon dioxide to fight fires.  Clifford came up with a patentable idea, and sold it to the fire company for $15,000.<ref name="Profile"/> With the money the Hachs co-founded [[Hach Company|Hach Chemical Company]] in 1947.<ref name=CEN2012 /> They bought an acre of land in Ames, Iowa, and built a cement block building which became their plant. They lived with their three children in a small apartment at the plant.<ref name="Profile"/><ref name=CEN2012 />

Clifford Hach was in charge of research and development while Kitty handled management and marketing.<ref name=CHFHachs /><ref name=Icons /> Their first successful product was a simplified titration method for measuring hardness in drinking water, which they packaged in easy-to-use testing kits. As municipal standards for drinking water were developed, Kitty recognized both the importance of water plant operators as a market, and the need to work closely with them to develop standards and provide long-term customer service.<ref name=Icons /> She developed a direct mail marketing campaign, and earned the nickname "Kitty" Hach by flying her plane across the United States, sometimes landing on rural dirt airstrips in bad weather, delivering water quality testing kits to municipalities of all sizes.<ref name="Profile"/><ref name=CHFOralHistory /> She became a member of the [[Ninety-Nines]], an international organization of licensed women pilots, and accumulated over 7,000 hours flying time.<ref name=ColoDegree /> She was rated for multi-engine and instrument flying.<ref name=NorthwoodArchive />

Kathryn Hach became the first woman director of the [[American Water Works Association]], an international non-profit, scientific and educational association founded to improve water quality and supply throughout the world.<ref name=HallOfFame>{{cite web|title=Kathryn Hach-Darrow|url=http://www.coloradobusinesshalloffame.org/kathryn-hach-darrow.html|publisher=Colorado Business Hall of Fame|accessdate=25 February 2014}}</ref> She later served on numerous AWWA committees, including the President's Advisory Council.<ref name=PressRelease2002 />

==Hach Chemical Company==

[[File:Women in Chemistry KHD Hach Water purification Freshfly Photo3.jpg |thumb|right|220px| Hach Water Purification Testing]]
[[File:Hach Classroom Drinking Water Testing Kit 2006.526 open.jpg|thumb|right|220px|Hach Classroom Drinking Water Testing Kit]]
Hach Chemical was instrumental in standardizing water-purification tests and pioneered many world-standard analytical instruments. Their tests were designed to be simple and effective, with nontechnical directions that made their products easy for both chemists and non-chemists to use. As of 2012, about 70 percent of municipalities in the United States used Hach Company instrumentation, allowing them to detect impurities in water at the parts-per-billion level.<ref name="Profile"/>

Hach Chemical Company was incorporated in 1951,<ref name=CHFOralHistory /> went public in 1968.<ref name=CEN2012 /> The company moved its headquarters to [[Loveland, Colorado]], in 1978,<ref name=Directory>{{cite web|title=Hach Co. History|url=http://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/hach-co-history/|publisher=International Directory of Company Histories|accessdate=26 February 2014}}</ref>   and was renamed [[Hach Company]] in 1980.<ref name=Icons /> Under Kitty Hach's management, the company developed an employee base of over 900 people and became one of the top women owned businesses in the United States.<ref name=HallOfFame /> Kathryn Hach-Darrow was president, chief operating officer, and CEO of the Hach company.<ref name=CHFPittcon2003 />

After Clifford's death in 1990, Kitty was named Hach Co.'s chairman and CEO and her son Bruce assumed the role of president.<ref name=Icons /> In 1995, she married Donald Darrow, a retired airline pilot, becoming Kitty Hach-Darrow. In 1999, Kitty and her son Bruce sold the Hach company to [[Danaher Corporation]].<ref name=CEN2012 />

==Awards and honors==

[[File:Kitty Hach Darrow, Arnold Thackray-2003 Pittcon Award.jpg|thumb|right|220px|Kitty Hach-Darrow receiving the 2003 Pittcon Heritage Award from Arnold Thackray, head of the [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]]]]

* In 1957, Kathryn and Clifford Hach jointly won the [[American Water (company)|American Water Works]] George Warren Fuller Award for distinguished service in the water supply field.<ref name=PressRelease2002 /><ref name=CHFPittcon2003>{{cite web|title= Pittcon Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/pittcon-heritage-award|website=Science History Institute|date=31 May 2016 |accessdate=21 March 2018}}</ref>  
* In 1987, the Hach Company was elected the Best Company in Colorado, receiving the award for the Northeastern part of the state.<ref name=NorthwoodArchive />
* In 1992, she was honored by [[Northwood University]] with an Outstanding Business Leaders Award.<ref name=NorthwoodArchive>{{cite web|title=Outstanding Business Leaders Archives|url=http://www.northwood.edu/about/honorees/outstanding-business-leaders-archive.aspx|publisher=Northwood University|accessdate=26 February 2014}}</ref><ref name=McCabe>{{cite news|last=McCabe|first=Robert|title=Students Meet Executives At Northwood Forum|url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1992-02-10/business/9201070929_1_carvel-business-leaders-annual-awards-dinner|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140314111239/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/1992-02-10/business/9201070929_1_carvel-business-leaders-annual-awards-dinner|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 14, 2014|accessdate=25 February 2014|newspaper=Sun Sentinel|date=10 February 1992}}</ref> 
* In January 2000, she was voted a member of the Colorado Business Hall of Fame (sponsored by the Denver Metro Chamber of Commerce and [[Junior Achievement]]).<ref name=HallOfFame /><ref name="CongressionalRecord">"2000 COLORADO BUSINESS HALL OF FAME INDUCTEE, KATHRYN 'KITTY' HACH-DARROW" in the ''Congressional Record'' (Bound Edition), Volume 146 (2000), Part 1, Page 449, U.S. Government Printing Office, Address by HON. SCOTT McINNIS of Colorado, Tuesday, February 1, 2000</ref><ref name=BizJournal>{{cite news|title=Business Hall of Fame makes room for 7 more|url=http://www.bizjournals.com/denver/stories/2000/01/17/story7.html?page=all|accessdate=26 February 2014|newspaper=Business Journal|date=16 January 2000}}</ref>
* Kathryn "Kitty" Hach-Darrow received the second annual [[Pittcon Heritage Award]] in 2003.<ref name=PressRelease2002>{{cite news|last=Gussman|first=Neil|title=CHF and Pittcon to present the Pittcon Heritage Award to Kathryn Hach-Darrow|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2002-10/chf-cap102302.php|accessdate=25 February 2014|newspaper=Chemical Heritage Foundation|date=23 October 2002|archive-date=22 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140322001933/http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2002-10/chf-cap102302.php|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=CHFPittcon2003 />
* In 2004, Kitty Hach-Darrow received the honorary degree of [[Doctor of Humane Letters]] from [[Colorado State University]].<ref name=ColoDegree>{{cite news|last=Ciaravola|first=Dell Rae|title=Colorado State University Awards Two Honorary Degrees During Fall Commencement Ceremonies|url=http://www.news.colostate.edu/Release/740|accessdate=26 February 2014|newspaper=Colorado State University News and Information|date=15 December 2004|archive-date=15 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140915232741/http://www.news.colostate.edu/Release/740|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Philanthropy==

* In 1982 the Hachs established the Hach Scientific Foundation to support chemistry in the classroom through grants to students and schools. In January 2009, the Hach Scientific Foundation transferred its assets to the [[American Chemical Society]], which continues to administer the scholarship and grant programs.<ref name=ACS-Hach>{{cite web|title=ACS-Hach Programs|url=http://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/hachprograms.html|publisher=American Chemical Society|accessdate=25 February 2014}}</ref><ref name="ACSObituary">{{cite web |title=Kitty Hach-Darrow, entrepreneur and philanthropist, dies at 97 |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2020/june/kitty-hach-darrow-entrepreneur-and-philanthropist-dies-at-97.html |website=American Chemical Society |accessdate=12 June 2020|date=June 11, 2020}}</ref>
* In May 2000, Kathryn Hach-Darrow gave a $10 million gift to [[Northwood University]]. The Hach Student Life Center, a 62,212 square foot student center which includes classrooms, social areas, and sports facilities, opened in 2002.<ref name=StudentCenter>{{cite news|title=Northwood invites public to building dedications|url=http://www.ourmidland.com/import/northwood-invites-public-to-building-dedications/article_c1863f59-8552-549a-bc5b-ce13b35b1750.html|accessdate=25 February 2014|newspaper=Midland Daily News|date=13 October 2002}}</ref> 
* Kitty Hach-Darrow and the Hach family were significant contributors to the building of Hach Hall, a new chemistry building dedicated at [[Iowa State University]] on October 8, 2010.<ref name=HachHall2010>{{cite news|title=Iowa State's chemistry department expects big boost from $78 million Hach Hall|url=http://www.news.iastate.edu/news/2010/aug/hachhall|accessdate=25 February 2014|newspaper=Iowa State University News Service|date=4 August 2010}}</ref>
* Through gifts in 2012 and 2014, Hach-Darrow established an endowment for the Kathryn C. Hach Award for Entrepreneurial Success through the American Chemical Society.  The award is to be given to someone who has "created something where nothing existed before”.<ref name="CENObituary"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Kathryn C. Hach Award for Entrepreneurial Success |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/entrepreneurial-success.html |website=American Chemical Society |accessdate=12 June 2020}}</ref>
